statement: For every n >= 4 there exists a self-complementary graph on n vertices.
definitions: A simple graph G is self-complementary if G is isomorphic to its complement (same vertex set, edges exactly the non-edges of G). A refutation must name an n >= 4 and show no self-complementary graph on n vertices exists.
ground_truth_witness: n = 6. No graph on 6 vertices is isomorphic to its complement: a self-complementary graph on n vertices must have exactly n(n-1)/4 edges, and for n = 6 that is 15/2, not an integer. (Self-complementary graphs exist exactly when n = 0 or 1 mod 4, e.g. P4 = 0-1-2-3 for n = 4 and C5 for n = 5, but none for n = 6 or 7.)

skeptic.objection: Precise and false: a self-complementary graph on n vertices needs exactly n(n-1)/4 edges, and 6*5/4 = 15/2 is not an integer (likewise n=7). The refutation is a genuine, if short, counting argument rather than naming an object, and the topic (self-complementary graphs) is absent from the roster. Low difficulty; suitable only if the set wants a warm-up item.
